editorial.headline: The Platform That Connects the Sale Without Owning the Goods
editorial.standfirst: A retail marketplace can be nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet its route through Bali depends on the precise scope declared in OSS.
editorial.body:
At its core, this is the business of running the digital meeting place for a retail transaction. The platform—whether a website or mobile application—brings sellers and buyers together so a good can be ordered. Its economic role is intermediation: it earns compensation or a commission, paid by the seller or the buyer, without supplying the goods or taking ownership of those it intermediates. That distinction gives the activity its centre of gravity. The operator enables the sale; it is not the merchant of the goods moving through the platform.

The scope is broad, but it is not indiscriminate. Its text expressly sets out exceptions involving PPMSE and PSP operators, both for those based within Indonesia and those based outside Indonesia that conduct electronic-commerce business in the country. For the activity as recorded, the available business scales run from Mikro and Kecil through Menengah to Besar. That breadth matters: the classification is not framed as a large-platform category alone, nor as a category reserved for an early-stage operator. It follows the practical function of the platform—facilitating a retail order for a commission—rather than the scale at which that function begins.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is direct. The activity is TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain terms, the national record permits full foreign ownership. That is the national position for this activity, supported by the cited presidential-regulation source. It should be read alongside the defined role of the platform: foreign participation is open for an operator whose business is to connect retail sellers and buyers for orders, while remaining outside the supply and ownership of the goods themselves.

Bali requires a more exact reading. The record does not mark the activity as outright blocked for PMA registration, but classifies the outcome as dependent on scope. Bali’s permanent, island-wide rule blocks PMA registration for all low- and medium-low-risk KBLI activities. At the Besar scale, however, the OSS risk can be low for some scopes and higher for others. The stated route for PMA registration in Bali is therefore to declare the higher-risk scope, with PPMSE given as the relevant platform-trade example. A national 100% ceiling remains meaningful, but it does not settle the Bali filing by itself: the exact activity declaration must be checked live in OSS.
editorial.pullQuote: A national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling is an opening, not a substitute for the precise Bali scope that OSS accepts.
